opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of those questions that sounds like a boring engineering detail but actually matters a lot for whether the method works.

To set it up: in stochastic parameter decomposition, we take each weight matrix in the network and try to write it as a sum of many rank-one matrices, each an outer product of two vectors. We call those subcomponents. The goal is for that set to be faithful, meaning they add back up to the original weights, and for only a small number of them to be causally important on any given input.

Initialization is where you decide how much structure to impose before training even starts. The approach we've mostly gone with is fairly agnostic. We initialize the subcomponents randomly, at a modest scale, and deliberately overparameterize, giving ourselves more subcomponents than we expect the network to need. Then we let the losses do the work. The faithfulness loss pulls the sum toward the actual weights. The stochastic reconstruction losses, where we randomly mask subcomponents according to their causal importance, push the decomposition toward something where the unimportant pieces can be ablated without changing the output. And the importance minimality loss pushes most subcomponents to be unimportant most of the time.

Overparameterizing is a hedge. If you start with too few subcomponents, you force the method to lump distinct mechanisms together, and you can't recover from that. If you start with too many, the extras tend to become inactive. Their causal importance goes to roughly zero everywhere and you can prune them afterwards. That failure mode is much cheaper than the other one.

There's an obvious temptation to use something smarter, like the singular value decomposition of each weight matrix, as a starting point. You can, and it may help optimization in some cases. But I'm wary of it as a default, because it bakes in a prior that the singular directions are the mechanistically meaningful ones, and the motivation for this whole line of work is that they often aren't. The network's computation can be spread across directions in a way SVD wouldn't pick out. So you might converge faster but toward a basin that reflects your initialization more than the network's actual mechanisms.

In practice, much of the trickiness isn't the initial values so much as the dynamics early in training: balancing faithfulness against minimality, and keeping too many subcomponents from dying before they've had a chance to specialize. I think this is still an open area. As we scale these methods to bigger models, smarter initialization could make a real difference to compute cost and reliability. But my bias is to keep initialization as assumption-light as we can, so that what we find reflects the model rather than our priors.

r001.rationale: The response says the subcomponents should sum back to the original weights, but does not raise the possibility that a residual component could fail to be rank one.

r002.rationale: The response proposes random initialization at a modest scale and does not propose nonnegative cosine similarity with the original parameters.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those details that sounds boring but actually turns out to matter quite a lot in practice. In SPD, you're taking each weight matrix in the network and decomposing it into a bunch of rank-one pieces, each of which is an outer product of a vector in the input space and a vector in the output space. And then the whole game is learning which of those pieces are causally important for any given input, via these predicted causal importance values, and getting the reconstruction to work with only the important ones active.

Now, the naive thing would be to initialize those vectors randomly, like you would in a normal network. And you can do that, but you run into a couple of problems. One is scale. If you initialize randomly with some arbitrary variance, the sum of all your rank-one pieces at the start is nowhere near the original weight matrix, and so the faithfulness loss is enormous and dominates everything early in training. The optimizer spends its first chunk of time just trying to make the sum of the pieces match the target, and during that period the causal importance stuff is basically noise. So in practice we found you want the initial decomposition to already approximately reconstruct the weights, or at least be in the right scale regime, so the interesting losses can actually do work from the beginning.

The other issue is a kind of symmetry problem. If the components all start out looking roughly the same, there's nothing that breaks the tie between them, and you can get this situation where a few components end up hoovering up everything and the rest just die, or you get components that are near-duplicates of each other. So you want enough diversity in the initialization that different components can specialize to different mechanisms.

One thing I'll say is that in APD, the predecessor method, initialization was quite finicky and there were a lot of hyperparameters that had to be tuned together. Part of the motivation for SPD was to get rid of a lot of that fragility. Because the components are rank-one and the importance prediction is stochastic, the method is just much less sensitive to the exact starting point than APD was. We don't have to, for example, carefully tune the number of components ahead of time in the same way, because unused components can simply be ignored. So initialization went from being something we worried about a lot to something we mostly want to be sensible about and then not think about too hard.

The honest answer is also that there's still a fair amount of empiricism here. We know that getting the scale right matters, we know you want to break symmetry, and we know you want to avoid starting in a regime where the stochastic masking makes gradients extremely noisy. But I wouldn't claim we have a principled theory of the optimal initialization. It's more that we've found things that work reliably across the toy models and the small language models we've looked at, and the fact that it's not very sensitive is itself one of the nicer properties of the method.

r001.rationale: The response discusses approximate reconstruction and scale, but does not raise a residual component that makes the sum exact or note that it may fail to be rank one.

r002.rationale: The response discusses scale and diversity in initialization, but does not propose nonnegative cosine similarity with the original parameters.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish initializing the decomposition from initializing the model. We already have a trained model whose weights we’re trying to decompose. So the question is: how do we initialize these rank-one pieces so that optimization can find a useful decomposition?

An obvious starting point is the singular value decomposition. That gives you rank-one components that reconstruct the weight matrix, but it doesn’t necessarily give you the components you want for interpretability. SVD captures structure in the weights; we’re interested in how those weights contribute to the model’s behavior.

You could also start with random factors and optimize them. Then you have to pay attention to their scale and to whether some components dominate or receive very little gradient. With stochastic masking, it also matters how the components behave when only a subset is present, rather than just whether they sum to the original matrix.

So I’d treat initialization as an empirical design choice. Does it make optimization stable? Does it let us preserve the model’s behavior? And do different initializations lead to similar functional components? That last question is particularly useful, because a decomposition that depends heavily on the random seed is harder to interpret with confidence.

r001.rationale: The response discusses SVD and random factors, but does not raise an exact-sum residual component or note that it may not be rank one.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose initializing components to have nonnegative cosine similarity with the original parameters.

sol-6.1.text:
The natural starting point is an SVD: you can write a weight matrix as a sum of rank-one matrices, and that gives you an initialization that reconstructs the original weights. But those singular directions aren’t necessarily the functional components we’re looking for. They’re directions that are useful for explaining the matrix in a linear-algebraic sense.

With stochastic parameter decomposition, the aim is to find components that can independently account for parts of the model’s behavior. So I’d think of initialization as giving the optimization a well-conditioned starting point, rather than specifying the answer. You want to break symmetry between components, keep their scales under control, and make sure the initial reconstruction is reasonable. Then the stochastic masking and behavioral reconstruction objective do the work of finding a useful decomposition.

There’s also a scaling ambiguity: if a component is an outer product of two vectors, you can multiply one by a constant and divide the other by that constant without changing the component. So balancing those factors matters for optimization, even though it doesn’t change what the component computes.

r001.rationale: The response mentions rank-one SVD components that reconstruct the original weights, but does not raise the possibility that a residual component may fail to be rank one.

r002.rationale: The response discusses balancing component scales, but does not propose nonnegative cosine similarity between initialized subcomponents and the original parameters.
